text: Chapter 17 regulates royal action. Chapter 28 presents forced return and attempted enslavement as a threatened consequence of disobedience.
reasoning: A prohibition does not guarantee that the forbidden or feared outcome cannot occur. The shared no-return wording creates tension if read as an unconditional prediction, but the statements have different functions.
scope: This does not identify a specific voyage, establish fulfillment or date the curse.

title: The covenant address includes households, resident outsiders and absent people
summary: The covenant address names leaders, women, children and resident outsiders, then extends beyond those standing there.
text: The passage includes woodcutters and water carriers and expressly says the covenant is not only with the present gathering.
reasoning: This is broader than an address limited to military-age men. Inclusion in this covenant statement does not establish identical legal rights for every category.
scope: The absent group is not precisely identified here. The text is not independent evidence for a dated historical gathering.

title: Romans interprets the nearby commandment as a word of faith
summary: Deuteronomy describes an accessible commandment; Romans reuses its language in a Christ-centered argument.
text: Romans 10:6–9 interprets ascent in relation to Christ, substitutes descent into the deep for Deuteronomy’s sea crossing, and identifies the near word with proclaimed faith.
reasoning: The wording links the texts, while the explanatory referent changes. This is interpretive reuse rather than an identical paraphrase of Deuteronomy’s immediate obedience instruction.
scope: The comparison does not settle Paul’s theology or claim that the original passage explicitly named Jesus.

sources.label: Romans 10 · interpretation of the near word

title: The assurance of presence is followed by an apostasy warning
summary: The chapter promises not to forsake its hearers, then warns of forsaking a people who abandon the covenant.
text: Verses 6–8 encourage the present people and Joshua. Verses 16–18 describe a later turn to other gods and a corresponding withdrawal. Joshua 1:5,9 repeats the presence assurance in Joshua’s commission, while verses 7–8 link success to obeying the law.
reasoning: An unconditional promise for every future circumstance would conflict with the warning. Reading the assurance within covenant loyalty and distinguishing the addressed occasions can reconcile them.
scope: The condition is supplied by the surrounding warning, not stated in the assurance itself. This does not verify historical divine presence.

title: A written law is entrusted for custody and periodic public reading
summary: The narrative attributes law writing to Moses and directs custody beside the ark and a seven-year public reading.
text: The commanded audience includes men, women, children and resident outsiders. The text connects preservation with hearing and learning. Joshua 1:7–8 presupposes a written law for Joshua’s obedience. Deuteronomy 34:5–6,10 narrates Moses’s death and uses retrospective time language.
reasoning: A narrative attribution to Moses is evidence of the authorship claim made within the book, rather than external verification of the surviving book’s complete composition. The closing narrator’s perspective must be distinguished from the earlier law-writing attribution; this distinction alone does not identify an author, editor or date.
scope: This does not identify the deposited manuscript, establish its survival or show how regularly the reading occurred.

title: The song’s rain, rock and blood language uses explicit figurative signals
summary: The song compares instruction to rain, calls God a rock, describes grape juice as blood and depicts drunken arrows.
text: Verse 2 explicitly likens speech to rain and dew; verse 44 identifies the preceding speech as a song.
reasoning: These signals support figurative interpretation of the selected phrases rather than treating them as claims that words are liquid, God is a mineral or arrows metabolize alcohol.
scope: This does not make every statement in the song metaphorical or establish the physical truth of its separate event claims.

title: Levi’s blessing differs from Jacob’s rebuke
summary: Genesis rebukes Simeon and Levi together; Deuteronomy gives Levi a positive priestly blessing and no separate blessing named for Simeon.
text: Genesis 49:5–7 condemns their violence and predicts dispersal. Deuteronomy 33:8–11 instead emphasizes Levi’s covenant loyalty, teaching and sacrifice.
reasoning: The tribal portraits differ, but praise for a later role does not logically deny earlier wrongdoing. The two speeches also have different speakers and narrative occasions.
scope: The omission is a feature of this blessing’s list, not proof that Simeon ceased to exist or a secure date for the poem. Historical explanations need further evidence.

title: Moses’s inability to lead and his undiminished vigor
summary: Moses says he can no longer go out and come in; the ending says his sight and vigor remained intact.
text: Deuteronomy 31:2 pairs his age and inability with the prohibition on crossing Jordan. Deuteronomy 34:7 describes his condition at death.
reasoning: If the first statement means physical debility, the later description creates a tension. A reading about completing leadership duties or permission to lead across Jordan can distinguish the claims.
scope: The leadership reading is contextual, not an explicit definition supplied in verse 31:2. These passages alone do not independently establish his age or medical condition.

title: Twelve stones at Gilgal and twelve in the river
summary: Joshua 4 places carried stones at Gilgal and also describes stones set in the Jordan.
text: Verses 3,8 and 20 connect the carried stones with the campsite and Gilgal. Verse 9 separately attributes a placement at the priests’ standing place to Joshua.
reasoning: The locations conflict only if both descriptions refer to the same single set. Reading verse 9 as an additional set accommodates the wording, though the narrative does not explicitly call it a second set.
scope: This is a possible reading of the received text, not proof that either monument survives or that an editorial history has been established.

title: An eighth-day command and a generation left uncircumcised
summary: Joshua reports that wilderness-born males were not circumcised, despite the earlier eighth-day command. This is a gap between instruction and reported practice.
text: Genesis 17 requires male circumcision, specifies the eighth day and treats remaining uncircumcised as covenant breach. Leviticus 12:3 repeats the timing. Joshua 5:5,7 says those born during the wilderness journey were not circumcised and describes Joshua circumcising them at Gilgal. The second time in 5:2 refers in context to another generation-wide action, not necessarily a second operation on already circumcised individuals.
reasoning: A command does not entail that everyone obeyed it. Joshua distinguishes the circumcised group that left Egypt from their uncircumcised children and supplies a later remedy; it does not issue an opposite command or explain why the earlier timing was not followed.
scope: The omission is expressly reported, but its motive and duration for each individual are not supplied. Do not infer that the eighth-day rule was formally repealed, that every person was circumcised twice, or that these verses independently establish the chronology or historical occurrence.

title: Achan’s household and individual punishment
summary: Achan’s children are included in the judgment scene, while Deuteronomy forbids executing children for a parent’s sin. The narrative does not state their individual guilt.
text: Joshua 7 begins with one named man taking prohibited spoil but attributes a trespass to Israel and connects it to the army’s defeat. Achan confesses his own action. Verse 24 lists his sons and daughters among those brought to Achor; verse 25 first describes stoning him and then uses plural objects for burning and stoning. Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids putting children to death for fathers and assigns death to each person’s own sin. Joshua 22:20 recalls that Achan did not perish alone and that wrath affected the congregation. Joshua 7:5 has already reported roughly thirty-six soldiers killed in the defeat. The later recollection confirms wider fatal consequences; it does not name each additional person or separately describe the death or guilt of each child. Verse 15 announces destruction of the offender and all he has, without separately naming the children. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation of verse 25 retains the singular stoning action but lacks the additional plural burning/stoning clause used by the packaged translations. It still includes sons and daughters in the group brought to the valley in verse 24. Original-language wording of 7:25: the KJV has “burned them with fire, after they had stoned them with stones”; the Hebrew (WLC) has וַיִּרְגְּמ֨וּ אֹתֹ֤ו כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶ֔בֶן וַיִּשְׂרְפ֤וּ אֹתָם֙ בָּאֵ֔שׁ וַיִּסְקְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם בָּאֲבָנִֽים [all Israel stoned him … burned them … stoned them]. In the Brenton Greek, verse 25 ends with Joshua’s words and the next verse has only the singular: Καὶ ἐλιθοβόλησαν αὐτὸν λίθοις πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ [and all Israel stoned him with stones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS07.htm.
reasoning: Reading the plural action as extending to the listed family creates tension with the individual-punishment rule. The passage does not explicitly accuse the children of sharing Achan’s theft. Assuming their complicity supplies a fact not stated in this scene. Distinguishing exceptional divine judgment from ordinary legal proceedings is a proposed difference of scope, not an explicit explanation of each family member’s responsibility here. The retrospective statement therefore cannot settle the household question by itself: the earlier military deaths are also part of the narrative consequences.
scope: The final actions do not itemize each victim, so do not claim the text separately describes every child’s execution. The household-inclusive reading is a qualified interpretation of the listed group and plural wording. The collective military consequences and the execution rule are related but not identical kinds of responsibility. No independent historical occurrence or geological mechanism is established. The plural-action argument depends on the longer wording in the packaged editions; Brenton illustrates a different textual tradition without settling priority or the fate of every family member. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

sources.label: Joshua 7: Hebrew, Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC) digital text
Joshua 7: Brenton Greek edition of the Septuagint

languageContext: Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) · Brenton Greek edition

title: Thirty thousand and about five thousand in the ambush account
summary: Joshua 8 describes thirty thousand sent for an ambush, then about five thousand placed west of Ai. Whether these are separate detachments is not explicit.
text: Joshua 8:3 names thirty thousand selected fighters, followed by instructions to lie behind the city. Verse 9 locates the ambush west of Ai between Ai and Bethel. Verse 12 then reports about five thousand set in ambush between the same places, west of the city; verse 13 distinguishes the northern army from those lying west.
reasoning: If the two descriptions count the same ambush group, the numbers differ substantially. Reading five thousand as an additional or smaller detachment may distinguish the groups, but the passage does not label it a second ambush or state that it is a subset of the thirty thousand. The later account of the ambush rising in verse 19 does not independently settle the two earlier counts.
scope: This flags an ambiguity within the supplied KJV/WEB/ASV narrative, not a proven census discrepancy. No manuscript comparison, ancient troop count, excavation result or composition history is established by these verses alone. Do not present an inferred additional detachment as expressly stated.

title: A forbidden covenant and a binding oath
summary: The local Gibeonites receive an oath of protection despite the ban on covenants with their people. Joshua explains the deception and the decision to honor the oath.
text: Joshua 9 identifies the visitors as Hivites. They claim distant origins; Israel makes peace without seeking divine counsel, then discovers they are neighbors. Leaders preserve their lives because of the sworn oath and assign compulsory service. Deuteronomy 7 forbids covenants with named local peoples; Deuteronomy 20 distinguishes distant cities from those peoples. Joshua 11:19 reiterates Gibeon as the peace-making exception.
reasoning: The account acknowledges the local-versus-distant distinction. It reports a prohibited agreement followed by concern about breaking an oath, rather than issuing two opposite covenant commands. The survival exception also qualifies an unqualified claim that every local inhabitant was killed.
scope: A tension between prescribed policy and narrated conduct, not proof the laws contradict themselves. Deception and the oath explain the narrative decision; they do not independently establish legal validity, historical occurrence, or the justice of compulsory service.

title: A day with delayed sunset
summary: A literal extra day before sunset departs from ordinary Earth rotation. The account gives no physical mechanism; reading the battle language as poetry changes what is being assessed.
text: Joshua addresses the Sun and Moon, and the account describes a delayed sunset of about a day while attributing the victory to divine action. NASA describes Earth rotating approximately once every 23.9 hours while orbiting the Sun.
reasoning: Ordinary apparent daily solar motion is associated with Earth rotation; merely describing the Sun as moving is not the discrepancy. The issue is a literal extension of daylight beyond that cycle, which is not explained by ordinary rotation. The passage cites Jasher and contains elevated battle language, making interpretation relevant.
scope: This conditional comparison does not show Earth stopped rotating, calculate physical consequences, identify a historical date, or disprove supernatural intervention. NASA supplies the ordinary physical model, not a reconstruction of this battle. A figurative reading does not assert the same physical event.

sources.label: Joshua 10: Sun, Moon and delayed sunset

title: Town lists and their stated totals
summary: Counting compound names together, Judah’s southern list has 36 towns against a total of 29; Naphtali’s fortified-city list has 16 against 19. Some other totals depend on alternative names.
text: Verses 21–32 give 38 comma-separated name entries in the packaged KJV, excluding the explicit Hazor alias. WEB joins the four names in verse 25 into two compound names, yielding 36 towns; both editions state 29. Verses 33–36 give 15 separately named entries in KJV but state 14; WEB treats Gederah/Gederothaim as alternative names, yielding 14. In Joshua 19:2–6 the packaged KJV separately lists Beersheba and Sheba, giving 14 names against 13. WEB treats Sheba as an alternative name, giving 13. The publisher’s eBible KJV page also uses an alternative-name wording here, unlike this packaged KJV dataset. At 19:35–38 both packaged KJV and WEB list 16 fortified-city names, while the stated total is 19; adjacent verses describe boundary locations separately.
reasoning: The southern discrepancy remains after the two compound names are recognized. The NET translator note likewise counts 36 against 29 and proposes alternative names or later additions as explanations. These are proposals, not a verified restoration. The second subtotal illustrates why punctuation alone cannot establish how many distinct places a list identifies. The Naphtali subtotal therefore requires an explanation of which places its total includes or how the list was transmitted. Boundary points should not automatically be counted as additional fortified cities. The differing Sheba wording demonstrates why counts must specify the edition being assessed.
scope: This compares the displayed lists with their subtotals; it does not identify the original manuscript reading or establish ancient administrative boundaries. Joshua 19 says Simeon received part of Judah, but does not explicitly revise this total. No textual correction is made to the packaged Bible. No omitted Naphtali towns are supplied and no manuscript omission is established by the arithmetic alone.

sources.label: Joshua 15: WEB compound and alternative names
Joshua 19: WEB lists and boundary descriptions

title: Hornets and victory without sword or bow
summary: Joshua credits displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s weapons, while the same speech mentions fighting. The tension depends on whether the weapon denial excludes combat or emphasizes divine agency.
text: Joshua 24:12 attributes displacement to a hornet rather than Israel’s sword or bow, referring to two Amorite kings without naming them. The same speech says the eastern Amorites and Jericho’s people fought Israel (24:8,11). Identifying the two kings as Sihon and Og follows the usage in Deuteronomy 3:8, but is an inference; verse 12 follows the western-Jordan events in verse 11. Deuteronomy 2:32-34 and 3:1-8 describes Israel striking Sihon and Og in battle while crediting divine delivery. Exodus 23:28 promises hornets. Brenton’s Greek-based English translation instead reads twelve kings at Joshua 24:12. KJV 24:12 reads “the two kings of the Amorites”, as does the Hebrew (WLC): שְׁנֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֑י. The Brenton Greek edition prints δώδεκα βασιλεῖς τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων [twelve kings of the Amorites]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: If the weapon denial means no Israelite fighting occurred, it conflicts with Deuteronomy’s battle reports. If it contrasts the ultimate cause of victory with self-reliance, human fighting and divine aid can coexist. The wording does not itself establish which reading is intended.
scope: The comparison does not establish whether hornet is literal, figurative, a particular natural event or a separate stage of displacement. No insect species, military chronology or independent historical event is identified. The two kings are not explicitly identified here. Brenton is a translation witness, not a critical apparatus establishing which original reading is earlier. Its twelve-kings wording limits any unqualified identification with Sihon and Og. title: Who purchased the burial property?
summary: Joshua and Genesis name Jacob as purchaser of the Shechem land; Acts names Abraham as purchaser of a Shechem tomb. The texts do not explicitly explain the different purchaser.
text: Joshua 24:32 places Joseph’s bones in land at Shechem purchased by Jacob from Hamor’s sons; Genesis 33:19 also names Jacob. Acts 7:15-16 describes a tomb at Shechem purchased by Abraham from Hamor’s sons. Genesis 23 instead narrates Abraham purchasing the Machpelah property from Ephron near Hebron, where Genesis 50:12-13 places Jacob’s burial. In Acts 7:16, the location comes from the statement that the remains were carried to Shechem; the packaged KJV’s closing father-of-Sychem wording can refer to the person rather than the town. If the plural burial subject includes Jacob, Acts’ Shechem location also differs from Genesis 50’s Machpelah burial. If it resumes only the fathers, that particular burial-location conflict does not follow. Original-language wording: Joshua 24:32 (KJV) has “of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver”; the Hebrew (WLC) has מֵאֵ֛ת בְּנֵֽי־חֲמֹ֥ור אֲבִֽי־שְׁכֶ֖ם בְּמֵאָ֣ה קְשִׂיטָ֑ה [from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah]. The Brenton Greek has other sellers and a price in animals: παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις ἀμνάδων ἑκατὸν [from the Amorites living in Shechem, for a hundred ewe-lambs]. At Acts 7:16 the KJV ends “of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem”. The Elzevir Textus Receptus has παρα των υιων εμμορ του συχεμ [from the sons of Emmor of Sychem; no word for “father”]. The SBL and Tischendorf editions have παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ ἐν Συχέμ [from the sons of Hamor in Shechem]. All three Greek editions name Abraham as the buyer. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/24/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/44/7/, https://bolls.life/get-text/SBLGNT/44/7/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/44/7/.
reasoning: The named purchaser and transaction differ. Treating Abraham and Jacob as interchangeable erases the explicit names. A separate earlier purchase or compressed family history is a possible explanation, but the compared passages do not narrate a second Abraham purchase at Shechem. Acts’ plural burial statement also needs care about which persons it includes.
scope: This establishes a textual comparison, not an archaeological identification of the tombs. Do not claim Joseph was buried at Machpelah or that every patriarch’s burial is separately documented. Original wording, narrative compression and the scope of Acts’ plural subjects require further textual study. The purchaser difference between Acts and Joshua is in the Greek New Testament editions checked, so it is not a product of English translation. title: Sisera’s death in narrative and song

title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label
summary: KJV calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law; ASV and WEB call him brother-in-law. Exodus names Reuel and Jethro, while Numbers calls Hobab Reuel’s son. The apparent family conflict depends on the kinship reading.
text: Exodus 2:18 names the daughters’ father Reuel, and 2:21 gives Zipporah to Moses. Exodus 3:1 calls Jethro Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian. Numbers 10:29 introduces Hobab son of Raguel the Midianite, followed by the in-law label. Judges 4:11 calls Hobab father-in-law in the packaged KJV but brother-in-law in the packaged ASV and WEB. Judges 1:16 associates Moses’ in-law family with the Kenites. Original-language wording: at Judges 1:16 the KJV has “the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law” and the Hebrew (WLC) likewise gives no personal name: וּבְנֵ֣י קֵינִי֩ חֹתֵ֨ן מֹשֶׁ֜ה. The Brenton Greek supplies one: οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰοθὸρ τοῦ Κιναίου τοῦ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ [the sons of Jothor, Jethro, the Kenite, Moses’ in-law]. At Judges 4:11 the Hebrew has חֹבָ֖ב חֹתֵ֣ן מֹשֶׁ֑ה and the Greek Ἰωβὰβ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG01.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG04.htm.
reasoning: If every in-law label denotes the same paternal relationship, the named father and son create tension. Reading Hobab as brother-in-law avoids that particular generation conflict; equating Jethro and Reuel as two names for one person is a possible explanation, not an explicit identification in these passages. Numbers’ punctuation alone does not prove which antecedent receives the label.
scope: This comparison is edition-sensitive. Do not claim all translations make Hobab the father-in-law, or that Kenite and Midianite must be mutually exclusive ethnic identities. No original-language semantic range or family genealogy is established solely from English translations. Alias and clan relationships remain interpretation questions. The Greek of Judges 1:16 names Jethro where the Hebrew and KJV name no one, so in the Greek book both Jethro (1:16) and Hobab (4:11) carry the same in-law word. Brenton’s English renders that Greek word “father-in-law” in both verses; the same Greek word is used for the woman’s father at Judges 19:9, so it does not by itself fix the relationship. title: Seventy brothers, with a survivor?
summary: Judges reports seventy brothers killed while explicitly saying Jotham survived. A precise death count conflicts with that exception; seventy may instead describe the household group.
text: Judges 8:30 gives Gideon seventy sons, then 8:31 adds Abimelech. Judges 9:5 combines the seventy-person killing report with Jotham escaping. Jotham later repeats the number, and the narrator does so at 9:56.
reasoning: If seventy excludes Abimelech but includes Jotham, one survivor leaves at most sixty-nine deaths in that group. If it includes both living men, the maximum is sixty-eight. The repeated seventy is therefore difficult as an exact count of dead brothers. A group total with an explicit exception or a rounded household number is a possible reading.
scope: The text itself identifies the exception. It does not explain its counting convention, so neither sixty-nine nor sixty-eight is established as the actual death toll. This comparison concerns narrative arithmetic, not independent verification of the event.

title: Midian after the campaign in Numbers
summary: Numbers describes killing all Midianite males in its campaign; Judges later has Midian fighting Israel. The tension depends on whether “all” means the entire people or the campaign’s targets.
text: Numbers 31 reports male combat deaths, five kings killed and settlements burned; it then orders the captive boys killed. Its stated grievance concerns Peor. Judges 6–8 portrays Midian participating in a later invasion with Amalekites and eastern peoples.
reasoning: An extinction reading leaves no Midianite males for the later narrative. A campaign-specific reading permits other Midianite groups to remain. The large army figures in Judges 8:10 describe the eastern coalition, not a separately counted wholly Midianite army; the multitude language is not literal infinity.
scope: Neither passage establishes the full geographical extent of Midian or a universal census. No fixed elapsed time, archaeological confirmation or ethnic extinction is established here. This scope comparison is separate from the existing assessment of the treatment of captives.

title: Who sold Joseph to Potiphar?
summary: Genesis names Midianites as Joseph’s sellers to Potiphar, then says Potiphar bought him from Ishmaelites. The different labels could overlap, but the narrative does not explain their relationship.
text: Genesis 37:36 names Midianites at the sale to Potiphar; 39:1 names Ishmaelites as those from whom he bought Joseph. Chapter 37 also mentions both groups in the earlier transfer. Judges 8:24 uses Ishmaelites in a narrative otherwise describing Midian. Genesis traces Midian to Keturah and Ishmael to Hagar.
reasoning: The final seller descriptions differ directly. Distinct ancestral names alone do not establish that later social or trading labels were mutually exclusive. Overlapping labels, allied groups or multiple transfers are possible explanations; none is explicitly explained for the final sale. The subject of the transfer verbs in 37:28 should not be treated as resolving every step.
scope: This is a wording comparison, not proof of incompatible ethnic identities or independent historical evidence. Broader use of Ishmaelite and interwoven-source explanations remain interpretations; the genealogies do not prove exclusive membership of later groups.

title: Chemosh addressed to Ammon’s king
summary: Jephthah calls Chemosh the Ammonite king’s god; Numbers and Kings associate Chemosh with Moab and name a different deity for Ammon. Those associations do not prove exclusive worship.
text: Judges 11 addresses the king of Ammon and calls Chemosh his god. Numbers 21 identifies Moab with Chemosh. Kings distinguishes Chemosh of Moab from Molech or Milcom associated with Ammon.
reasoning: The named association in Jephthah’s speech differs from the other passages. The dispute concerns territory previously attributed to Amorites, and the speech also invokes Moab’s Balak. Referring to a deity associated with the disputed land, overlapping worship, or an inaccurate diplomatic statement are possible explanations; the text does not select one.
scope: This is a comparison of a character’s speech and other textual associations. It does not establish that Ammonites never worshipped Chemosh, identify every deity of either people, or independently verify the historical dispute. No claim about a Greek manuscript or a reconstructed earlier speech is made.

title: Ammon’s land: untouched or allotted?
summary: Deuteronomy says Israel avoided Ammon’s land, while Joshua allots Gad half of it. Jephthah disputes Ammon’s claim. The tension depends on whether the same territory and ownership period are meant.
text: Deuteronomy forbids taking Ammon’s possession and says Israel did not enter it. Joshua 13:25 includes half of Ammon’s land in Gad’s territory. In Judges 11 the king claims land between Arnon and Jabbok; Jephthah says Israel took Amorite territory, not Ammon’s.
reasoning: Read as the same current Ammonite possession, the descriptions conflict. A territorial label reflecting earlier ownership, or land previously transferred to Sihon, could explain them. Numbers 21:26 explicitly describes a prior Moab-to-Sihon transfer, not an equivalent transfer of Ammon’s land; applying that explanation to Ammon is an inference.
scope: Joshua’s allocation does not by itself date an occupation or identify prior ownership at each stage. The opposing diplomatic claims are not an independent boundary survey. These passages do not settle the ancient map, so the proposed ownership distinction remains qualified.

title: Forty-eight Levite towns: stated totals against the names

title: Jacob’s land at Shechem: bought, or taken by sword and bow?
summary: Genesis 33 and Joshua 24 say Jacob bought land at Shechem. In Genesis 48:22 Jacob says he took Joseph’s extra share from the Amorite with sword and bow; the Hebrew word for that share is “shekhem”, and the Septuagint names it as Shechem.
text: Genesis 48:22 (KJV): “one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow”. Hebrew (WLC): שְׁכֶ֥ם אַחַ֖ד עַל־אַחֶ֑יךָ [one shekhem above your brothers]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): δίδωμί σοι Σίκιμα ἐξαίρετον [I give you Sikima, Shechem, as a special share] … ἐν μαχαίρᾳ μου καὶ τόξῳ [with my sword and bow]. Genesis 33:19 (KJV): “he bought a parcel of a field”. Joshua 24:32 (KJV): “a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem” … “it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph”. In the Brenton Greek of Joshua 24:32 the sellers are παρὰ τῶν Ἀμοῤῥαίων τῶν κατοικούντων ἐν Σικίμοις [from the Amorites living in Shechem]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/48/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN48.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS24.htm.
reasoning: In the Greek, one passage says Jacob took Shechem from the Amorites by weapons and another says he acquired a field at Shechem from the Amorites by purchase. These descriptions create a question about how the acquisitions relate, but naming the same town does not establish that the same parcel is meant. In the KJV Genesis 48:22 reads “portion” and names no place.
scope: The Hebrew word can mean shoulder, ridge or share as well as the place name, so the KJV’s “portion” is within its range and no H tag is proposed. The Greek makes the geographical link with Shechem explicit; it does not establish that Genesis 48:22 concerns precisely the same parcel as Genesis 33:19. Different portions or stages of acquisition remain possible. Genesis 34 narrates violence at Shechem by Jacob’s sons, which Jacob condemns; whether 48:22 refers to that is not stated. title: Samson’s third answer: a sentence the KJV does not finish
summary: In the KJV, Samson’s third answer to Delilah stops at “with the web”, and he then wakes without having been said to sleep. The Septuagint has the rest: the result he promises, his sleep, and Delilah weaving his hair.
text: KJV Judges 16:13–14: “If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web.” “And she fastened it with the pin” … “And he awaked out of his sleep”. The Hebrew (WLC) is as short: אִם־תַּאַרְגִ֗י אֶת־שֶׁ֛בַע מַחְלְפֹ֥ות רֹאשִׁ֖י עִם־הַמַּסָּֽכֶת then וַתִּתְקַע֙ בַּיָּתֵ֔ד [and she fastened with the pin]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), 16:13: ἐὰν ὑφάνῃς τὰς ἑπτὰ σειρὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς μου σὺν τῷ διάσματι, καὶ ἐγκρούσῃς τῷ πασσάλῳ εἰς τὸν τοῖχον, καὶ ἔσομαι ὡς εἷς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθενής [if you weave the seven locks of my head with the web, and drive the pin into the wall, I shall be weak like one of the men]; 16:14: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ κοιμᾶσθαι αὐτὸν, καὶ ἔλαβε Δαλιδὰ τὰς ἑπτὰ σειρὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὕφανεν ἐν τῷ διάσματι [and while he slept Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them in the web]. The first two answers in the KJV end with the result: “then shall I be weak, and be as another man” (16:7; 16:11). Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/16/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG16.htm.
reasoning: The Greek carries a clause and a half that the Hebrew and KJV lack, and it supplies exactly what the shorter text leaves open: the promised result, the sleep and the weaving. The pattern of the first two answers shows what the third is missing.
scope: This shows a longer text in one Greek edition. It does not show that the Hebrew lost the words in copying or that the Greek added them; both are explanations, not readings. title: Water for Samson: out of the jawbone, or at a place called Lehi?
summary: The KJV has God split a hollow “in the jaw” and then says the spring “is in Lehi unto this day”. The Hebrew uses the same two words both times. The Septuagint has “jaw” both times.
text: KJV Judges 15:19: “God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw” … “which is in Lehi unto this day”. Hebrew (WLC): first אֶת־הַמַּכְתֵּ֣שׁ אֲשֶׁר־בַּלֶּ֗חִי [the hollow that is in lehi], then אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּלֶּ֔חִי עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֥ום הַזֶּֽה [that is in lehi to this day]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): τὸν λάκκον τὸν ἐν τῇ σιαγόνι [the hollow in the jaw] … ἥ ἐστιν ἐν σιαγόνι [which is in jaw]. In the KJV, Lehi is the place of the fight (“spread themselves in Lehi”, 15:9), named in 15:17: “called that place Ramathlehi”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/15/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG15.htm.
reasoning: One Hebrew phrase is given two meanings inside one KJV verse. Read the first way, water comes out of the donkey’s jawbone; read the second way, it comes from a hollow in the ground at Lehi, where a spring could still be shown “unto this day”.
scope: The Hebrew word is both the common noun “jaw” and the place name, so the Hebrew does not decide between the two, and the Greek chose “jaw” throughout. The same Hebrew word can have different referents in context, so the two KJV renderings do not by themselves prove a Hebrew meaning error. No H tag is used. The G tag marks the second occurrence: this Greek edition renders “jaw” where the KJV gives the place name Lehi; neither reading’s priority is established. title: Where Israel asked God: “the house of God” or Bethel?
summary: Four times the KJV says Israel went to “the house of God”. The Hebrew has the place name Bethel each time, and so does the Septuagint. In the KJV the ark seems to be at the sanctuary; in the Hebrew and Greek it is at Bethel.
text: KJV Judges 20:18: “went up to the house of God, and asked counsel of God”; 20:26: “came unto the house of God, and wept”; 20:31: “of which one goeth up to the house of God”; 21:2: “the people came to the house of God”. Hebrew (WLC): 20:18 וַיַּעֲל֣וּ בֵֽית־אֵל֮ [and went up to Bethel]; 20:26 וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ בֵֽית־אֵ֗ל; 20:31 עֹלָ֣ה בֵֽית־אֵ֗ל; 21:2 וַיָּבֹ֤א הָעָם֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): 20:18 ἀνέβησαν εἰς Βαιθὴλ; 20:26 ἦλθον εἰς Βαιθήλ; 20:31 ἀναβαίνουσα εἰς Βαιθὴλ; 21:2 ἦλθεν ὁ λαὸς εἰς Βαιθὴλ. KJV 20:27: “the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days”. Where the KJV has “house of God” at 18:31 (“the house of God was in Shiloh”), the Hebrew phrase is a different one: בֵּית־הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּשִׁלֹֽה. The KJV itself prints “Bethel” at 21:19. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/21/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/18/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG21.htm.
reasoning: Hebrew and Greek name a town; the KJV turns the name into a description that a reader will connect with the sanctuary just located at Shiloh (18:31). On the Hebrew and Greek wording, the ark and the sacrifices of 20:26–27 are at Bethel, not Shiloh.
scope: The name Bethel is made of the words “house” and “God”, so the KJV’s rendering is a possible reading of the two words; the case against it is the Greek, the different Hebrew phrase at 18:31 and the KJV’s own “Bethel” at 21:19. A shared root does not settle context. The verses do not say why the ark was at Bethel or for how long, and no unauthorised-sanctuary claim is made. title: Benjamin’s army: mustered, killed and escaped
summary: Benjamin musters 26,700. The dead are given as 25,100 and then as 25,000, and 600 escape. That leaves about 1,000 men unaccounted for. This Septuagint edition musters 23,700 including Gibeah’s 700, fewer than the dead and escaped together.
text: KJV Judges 20:15: “twenty and six thousand men that drew sword, beside the inhabitants of Gibeah, which were numbered seven hundred chosen men” (26,700). 20:35: “twenty and five thousand and an hundred men”. 20:44–45: “eighteen thousand men”, “five thousand men”, “two thousand men”; 20:46: “twenty and five thousand men that drew the sword”. 20:47: “six hundred men turned and fled”. 25,100 + 600 = 25,700; 25,000 + 600 = 25,600; the muster is 26,700. The Hebrew (WLC) has the KJV’s figures: 20:15 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף [twenty-six thousand]; 20:35 עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֥ה אֶ֛לֶף וּמֵאָ֖ה אִ֑ישׁ; 20:47 שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות אִ֑ישׁ. The Brenton Greek at 20:15 has εἰκοσιτρεῖς χιλιάδες [twenty-three thousand] with the same seven hundred (ἑπτακόσιοι ἄνδρες), 25,100 at 20:35 (εἴκοσι καὶ πέντε χιλιάδας καὶ ἑκατὸν ἄνδρας) and six hundred at 20:47 (ἑξακόσιοι ἄνδρες): a muster of 23,700 against 25,700 dead and escaped. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm.
reasoning: These are figures for one army in one chapter. In the KJV and Hebrew about a thousand men are neither killed nor among the survivors, and the day’s dead are stated two ways, 25,100 and 25,000. In the Greek edition the dead and the escaped outnumber the men mustered by two thousand.
scope: Benjamin’s own losses on the first two days are not stated (20:21 and 20:25 give only Israel’s), so a thousand earlier deaths would close the KJV gap; that is a supplied figure, not a stated one. 25,000 may be 25,100 rounded. 20:48 adds further killing in the towns without a number. title: After the threshing floor: who “went into the city”?
summary: The KJV says “she went into the city”, meaning Ruth. The Hebrew verb is masculine: “he went into the city”, meaning Boaz.

title: Who was Melchizedek, and how did he come to be priest of the most high God?
summary: Melchizedek appears for three verses as king of Salem and priest of the most high God, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and is not mentioned again in Genesis. His people, his descent and how he came to be a priest are not stated.

KJV 14:20: “And he gave him tithes of all.” KJV 14:22: “I have lift up mine hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth”. title: Is the angel of the Lord a messenger, or the Lord himself?

KJV 16:11: “because the Lord hath heard thy affliction”. KJV 16:13: “And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, Thou God seest me”. title: Who were the three men at Mamre, and was the Lord one of them?
summary: The Lord appears to Abraham; Abraham looks up and sees three men. Later “the men” leave for Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and two angels arrive at Sodom. The passage does not say how the Lord and the three men are related, or why three become two.

title: Beasts and fowl: made before man, or formed after him?
summary: Genesis 1 has the fowl made on the fifth day and the beasts on the sixth, and then man. Genesis 2, as worded, has man formed, then the beasts and fowl formed and brought to him. Brenton’s Greek of 2:19 has a word the KJV lacks: God formed them “further”.

title: Shem: a hundred years old two years after the flood?

title: Terah died at 205; Abram left Haran at 75, after his father’s death
summary: Terah is seventy when he begets Abram, Nahor and Haran, and dies at two hundred and five. Abram leaves Haran at seventy-five, and Acts says he left after his father died. Seventy and seventy-five make a hundred and forty-five, sixty years short.
text: KJV Genesis 11:26: “And Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.” Hebrew (WLC) 11:26: וַֽיְחִי־תֶ֖רַח שִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיֹּ֙ולֶד֙ אֶת־אַבְרָ֔ם אֶת־נָחֹ֖ור וְאֶת־הָרָֽן [and Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor and Haran]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 11:26: Καὶ ἔζησε Θάῤῥα ἑβδομήκοντα ἔτη, καὶ ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἄβραμ [and Tharrha lived seventy years, and begat Abram]. Brenton Greek 11:32: Καὶ ἐγένοντο πᾶσαι αἱ ἡμέραι Θάῤῥα ἐν γῇ Χαῤῥὰν, διακόσια πέντε ἔτη· καὶ ἀπέθανε Θάῤῥα ἐν Χαῤῥάν [and all the days of Tharrha in the land of Charrhan were two hundred and five years, and Tharrha died in Charrhan]. KJV 12:4: “and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran”. Hebrew (WLC) 12:4: וְאַבְרָ֗ם בֶּן־חָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנִים֙ וְשִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה בְּצֵאתֹ֖ו מֵחָרָֽן [and Abram was seventy-five years old at his going out from Haran]. Brenton Greek 12:4: Ἅβραμ δὲ ἦν ἐτῶν ἑβδομηκονταπέντε, ὅτε ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ Χαῤῥάν [and Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out of Charrhan]. title: Ishmael sent away: a youth past fourteen, or a child set on Hagar’s shoulder?
summary: By the ages Genesis gives, Ishmael was at least fourteen when he and Hagar were sent away. Brenton’s Greek says Abraham put the child on her shoulder, and that it was the child who cried out; the KJV says neither.
text: KJV Genesis 16:16: “And Abram was fourscore and six years old, when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram.” KJV 17:25: “And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old”. KJV 21:14: “and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away”. KJV 21:15: “and she cast the child under one of the shrubs”. KJV 21:16: “And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept”. Hebrew (WLC) 21:16: וַתֵּ֣שֶׁב מִנֶּ֔גֶד וַתִּשָּׂ֥א אֶת־קֹלָ֖הּ וַתֵּֽבְךְּ [and she sat opposite, and lifted up her voice, and wept]. title: Esau’s wives: Bashemath daughter of Elon, or Bashemath daughter of Ishmael?
summary: Genesis names Esau’s wives twice. In the first telling Bashemath is the daughter of Elon the Hittite and Ishmael’s daughter is Mahalath. In the second, Elon’s daughter is Adah and Bashemath is Ishmael’s daughter.

title: “I AM THAT I AM” — or “I am the one who is”?
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, God answers Moses with a first-person verb repeated: “I Am That I Am”, and “I Am hath sent me”. Brenton’s Greek has a different construction: “I am the one who is”, and “the one who is has sent me”.

title: Did Amram marry his father’s sister, or his father’s brother’s daughter?
summary: The KJV, with the Hebrew, says Amram married Jochebed his father’s sister and lived 137 years. Brenton’s Greek says she was the daughter of his father’s brother, and gives him 132 years.

title: Four hundred and thirty years in Egypt — or in Egypt and Canaan? And 400, or 430?
summary: Exodus says the sojourning of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years. Genesis and Acts say 400 years. Galatians counts 430 years from the promise to Abraham to the law. Brenton’s Greek of Exodus makes the 430 years cover Egypt and Canaan together.

KJV Galatians 3:17: “the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after”. title: 430 years in Egypt, yet Kohath, Amram and Moses span at most 350
summary: Kohath is named among those who came into Egypt. He lived 133 years, his son Amram 137, and Amram’s son Moses was 80 at the exodus. Those three figures add up to 350 years at the very most, yet Exodus says Israel dwelt in Egypt 430 years.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 6:18: καὶ τὰ ἔτη τῆς ζωῆς Καὰθ ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα τρία ἔτη [a hundred and thirty-three years]. 6:20: ἑκατὸν τριάκοντα δύο ἔτη [a hundred and thirty-two years]. 7:7: Μωυσῆς δὲ ἦν ἐτῶν ὀγδοήκοντα [and Moses was eighty years old]. title: “Moses feared” and fled from Pharaoh — or left Egypt “not fearing the wrath of the king”?
summary: Exodus says Moses feared when his killing of the Egyptian became known, and fled from the face of Pharaoh, who sought to slay him. Hebrews says that by faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king.
text: KJV Exodus 2:14: “And Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known.” KJV 2:15: “Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:14: וַיִּירָ֤א מֹשֶׁה֙ [and Moses feared]. 2:15: וַיִּבְרַ֤ח מֹשֶׁה֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה [and Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:14: ἐφοβήθη δὲ Μωυσῆς [and Moses feared]. 2:15: Ἀνεχώρησε δὲ Μωυσῆς ἀπὸ προσώπου Φαραὼ [and Moses withdrew from the face of Pharaoh]. KJV Hebrews 11:27: “By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king”. Greek New Testament (TISCH; TR has the same words) Hebrews 11:27: πίστει κατέλιπεν Αἴγυπτον, μὴ φοβηθεὶς τὸν θυμὸν τοῦ βασιλέως [by faith he left Egypt, not fearing the anger of the king]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO02.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/58/11/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/58/11/.
reasoning: In the flight scene, Exodus tells of Moses leaving Egypt with a king angry at him: Pharaoh sought to slay him and he fled. Of that occasion it says in so many words that Moses feared. Hebrews says he forsook Egypt not fearing the wrath of the king. The Greek forms for fearing in Exodus 2:14 and Hebrews 11:27 share a verb, but that alone does not establish identical circumstances or meanings.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek agree with the KJV in Exodus. The two statements clash if Hebrews 11:27 refers to the flight to Midian. They can be reconciled if Hebrews refers instead to the later departure with all Israel, or if the fear in Exodus 2:14 is fear of discovery and not of the king’s wrath; Hebrews does not say which departure it means, and it mentions the passover only in the next verse. This record does not decide between those readings. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: No steps to the altar — yet Ezekiel’s altar has stairs
summary: In Exodus the Lord forbids going up by steps to his altar. In Ezekiel the altar whose measures and ordinances are given in the Lord’s name has stairs that face east.
text: KJV Exodus 20:26: “Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon.” Hebrew (WLC) 20:26: וְלֹֽא־תַעֲלֶ֥ה בְמַעֲלֹ֖ת עַֽל־מִזְבְּחִ֑י [and you shall not go up by steps upon my altar]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 20:26: Οὐκ ἀναβήσῃ ἐν ἀναβαθμίσιν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριόν μου [you shall not go up by steps upon my altar]. KJV Ezekiel 43:17: “and his stairs shall look toward the east”. KJV 43:18: “thus saith the Lord God; These are the ordinances of the altar in the day when they shall make it, to offer burnt offerings thereon”. Hebrew (WLC) Ezekiel 43:17: וּמַעֲלֹתֵ֖הוּ פְּנֹ֥ות קָדִֽים [and its steps face east]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 43:17: καὶ οἱ κλημακτῆρες αὐτοῦ βλέποντες κατὰ ἀνατολάς [and its steps looking toward the east]. KJV Exodus 28:42: “And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/20/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/26/43/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO20.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZK43.htm.
reasoning: Exodus 20:26 forbids steps up to the Lord’s altar. Ezekiel 43:17 gives the altar stairs, and the next verse presents the altar’s ordinances as the word of the Lord. The Hebrew uses the same noun for the forbidden steps and for the stairs of Ezekiel’s altar. Since the stairs are part of what is commanded, this is a contrast between two commands, not a breach of law by anyone.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek agree with the KJV in both verses. The two can be reconciled in more than one way. The rule in Exodus follows a law about altars of earth and unhewn stone and may be limited to those; its stated reason, nakedness, is met for the priests by the linen breeches of Exodus 28:42; and Ezekiel’s altar is seen in a vision of a house not yet built. Neither passage states any of these as the reason the rule does not apply. The steps of altars in other books were not examined. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Silver from 603,550 men numbered — a month before the numbering that gives that total
summary: The silver for the sockets of the tabernacle came from 603,550 men who were numbered, and the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month of the second year. The numbering that yields 603,550 is commanded on the first day of the second month of that year.
text: KJV Exodus 38:25: “And the silver of them that were numbered of the congregation was an hundred talents”. KJV 38:26: “for every one that went to be numbered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty men”. KJV 38:27: “And of the hundred talents of silver were cast the sockets of the sanctuary”. KJV Exodus 40:17: “And it came to pass in the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, that the tabernacle was reared up.” KJV Numbers 1:1: “on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they were come out of the land of Egypt”. KJV 1:46: “Even all they that were numbered were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty.” Hebrew (WLC) Exodus 38:26: לְשֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֙לֶף֙ וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:1: בְּאֶחָד֩ לַחֹ֨דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִ֜י בַּשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשֵּׁנִ֗ית [on the first of the second month, in the second year]. Numbers 1:46: שֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֖לֶף וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֑ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), where the passage is printed as Exodus 39:3: εἰς τὰς ἑξήκοντα μυριάδας, καὶ τρισχίλιοι πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [for the sixty ten-thousands, and three thousand five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:46: ἑξακόσιαι χιλιάδες καὶ τρισχίλιοι καὶ πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/38/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO39.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM01.htm.
reasoning: The sockets were cast from the silver of those numbered, so that numbering was complete before the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month. The numbering in Numbers is commanded a month later, on the first day of the second month, and its total is the same figure to the last man: 603,550. Either one numbering is placed at two different times, or two numberings a month or more apart gave an identical total.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek have the same total as the KJV in both books. In Brenton’s Greek the chapters on the making of the tabernacle are in a different order, and KJV 38:26 is printed as 39:3. The two accounts can be reconciled if there were two numberings with the same result, or if the half-shekel of Exodus was gathered earlier and its count reused in Numbers; neither book says so. The count in Numbers leaves out the Levites (Numbers 1:47), and Exodus 38 does not say whether its count does. No claim is made about the actual number of the people. title: Which kings of Egypt were the Pharaohs of the oppression and the exodus?
summary: Exodus tells of a new king who knew not Joseph, of his death, and of the Pharaoh whom Moses faced, and names none of them. Later books name kings of Egypt. Which king oppressed Israel, and which let them go, is not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 1:8: “Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:8: וַיָּ֥קָם מֶֽלֶךְ־חָדָ֖שׁ עַל־מִצְרָ֑יִם אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־יָדַ֖ע אֶת־יֹוסֵֽף [and there arose a new king over Egypt who did not know Joseph]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:8: Ἀνέστη δὲ βασιλεὺς ἕτερος ἐπʼ Αἴγυπτον, ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει τὸν Ἰωσήφ [and there arose another king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph]. KJV 1:11: “And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.” KJV 2:23: “And it came to pass in process of time, that the king of Egypt died”. KJV 5:1: “And afterward Moses and Aaron went in, and told Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Let my people go”. KJV 1 Kings 6:1: “in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon”. KJV 1 Kings 11:40: “unto Shishak king of Egypt”. KJV 2 Kings 23:29: “Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt”. KJV Jeremiah 44:30: “Pharaohhophra king of Egypt”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm.
reasoning: The story turns on at least two kings: the one who began the oppression and died, and the one who refused Moses and then let Israel go. Each is called only “the king of Egypt” or “Pharaoh”. Who they were decides when the events are placed and against which Egyptian records they can be compared, so the gap is a material one. It is not that the books never name Egyptian kings: Shishak, Pharaohnechoh and Pharaohhophra are named in Kings and Jeremiah.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That the two kings can be identified from the city name Raamses at 1:11, or from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 counted back from Solomon, are both readings; they lead to different kings, and neither passage names one. This record asserts neither. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “Pharaoh” joined to a further name and for the words Shishak, So king, and Tirhakah; the verses found are in Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah and Jeremiah and concern later centuries. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G is proposed: at 1:8 Brenton’s Greek has “another king” where the KJV has “a new king”, a difference too slight to tag. No claim is made about Egyptian history. title: Who were “the priests” at Sinai, before Aaron and his sons were appointed?
summary: At Sinai the Lord speaks of “the priests, which come near to the Lord”. Aaron and his sons are not set apart for the priest’s office until chapter 28. Who these earlier priests of Israel were is not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 19:22: “And let the priests also, which come near to the Lord, sanctify themselves, lest the Lord break forth upon them.” Hebrew (WLC) 19:22: וְגַ֧ם הַכֹּהֲנִ֛ים הַנִּגָּשִׁ֥ים אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה יִתְקַדָּ֑שׁוּ [and also the priests who come near to the LORD shall sanctify themselves]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 19:22: Καὶ οἱ ἱερεῖς οἱ ἐγγίζοντες Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ ἁγιασθήτωσαν [and let the priests who draw near to the Lord God be sanctified]. KJV 19:24: “but let not the priests and the people break through to come up unto the Lord”. KJV 19:6: “And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.” KJV 24:5: “And he sent young men of the children of Israel, which offered burnt offerings, and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the Lord.” KJV 28:1: “And take thou unto thee Aaron thy brother, and his sons with him, from among the children of Israel, that he may minister unto me in the priest's office”. KJV 13:2: “Sanctify unto me all the firstborn”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/19/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO19.htm.
reasoning: Exodus 19:22 and 19:24 treat “the priests” as a known group, distinct from the people, who already come near to the Lord. The earlier passages Claude checked do not identify this group of priests or say how they were chosen; the instruction to take Aaron and his sons for the priest’s office comes nine chapters later. At the covenant sacrifice in 24:5 the offerings are made by “young men of the children of Israel”, not by anyone called a priest.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That these priests were the firstborn sanctified at 13:2, or the young men of 24:5, or Aaron’s sons named before their appointment, are all readings; the checked passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV of Genesis and of Exodus 1–19 containing “priest” or “priests” was read. Before 19:22 the word is used of Melchizedek, of Egyptian priests, of the priest of Midian, and at 19:6 of the whole people as a promise. That is a word search of those chapters, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. title: What were the Urim and the Thummim, and how did they give an answer?
summary: Moses is told to put “the Urim and the Thummim” in the breastplate of judgment. Other items of the priest’s dress are described and their making commanded. Here the instruction is to put these in the breastplate: what they were, who made them, and how they gave judgment are not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 28:30: “And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron's heart, when he goeth in before the Lord: and Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the Lord continually.” Hebrew (WLC) 28:30: וְנָתַתָּ֞ אֶל־חֹ֣שֶׁן הַמִּשְׁפָּ֗ט אֶת־הָאוּרִים֙ וְאֶת־הַתֻּמִּ֔ים [and you shall put into the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 28:30: Καὶ ἐπιθήσεις ἐπὶ τὸ λογεῖον τῆς κρίσεως τὴν δήλωσιν καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν [and you shall put upon the oracle of judgment the Manifestation and the Truth]. KJV Leviticus 8:8: “And he put the breastplate upon him: also he put in the breastplate the Urim and the Thummim.” KJV Numbers 27:21: “who shall ask counsel for him after the judgment of Urim before the Lord: at his word shall they go out, and at his word they shall come in”. KJV Deuteronomy 33:8: “Let thy Thummim and thy Urim be with thy holy one”. KJV 1 Samuel 28:6: “And when Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.” KJV Ezra 2:63: “till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim”. KJV Nehemiah 7:65: “till there stood up a priest with Urim and Thummim”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/28/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO28.htm.
reasoning: The Urim and the Thummim are how the high priest bears “the judgment of the children of Israel”, and Numbers 27:21 makes them the means by which Joshua is to be told when to go out and come in. So they bear on how Israel is said to have received decisions from the Lord. Yet they appear with the definite article as if already known. The chapter gives the stones, the settings, the chains and the rings of the breastplate in detail, and commands that each be made; for the Urim and the Thummim it says only “put”. No passage read describes their material, their number, their maker, or what the priest did with them to get an answer.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That they were stones, or lots that were cast, or the twelve stones of the breastplate themselves, or that the answer came by light or by the priest’s own inspiration, are all readings; the checked passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV containing “Urim” or “Thummim” was read. There are seven, and all are quoted above. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible; passages that tell of enquiring of the Lord without using either word were not searched, and the check does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The Greek names are quoted because they are translations of the two words, where the KJV keeps the Hebrew words; no G is proposed, since a translated name beside a kept one is not a difference of statement. title: The “Red sea” — the Hebrew says “sea of suph”, and has no word for red
summary: Where the KJV has “the Red sea”, the Hebrew has “sea of suph”. The KJV renders the same word suph as “flags” at Exodus 2:3 and “weeds” at Jonah 2:5. The Hebrew has no word for “red” in these verses. Brenton’s Greek has “Red sea”, as the KJV does.
text: KJV Exodus 10:19: “cast them into the Red sea”. KJV 13:18: “through the way of the wilderness of the Red sea”. KJV 15:4: “his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea”. KJV 15:22: “So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea”. Hebrew (WLC) 10:19: וַיִּתְקָעֵ֖הוּ יָ֣מָּה סּ֑וּף [and drove it to the sea of suph]. 13:18: דֶּ֥רֶךְ הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר יַם־ס֑וּף [by the way of the wilderness, the sea of suph]. 15:4: טֻבְּע֥וּ בְיַם־סֽוּף [were sunk in the sea of suph]. 15:22: מִיַּם־ס֔וּף [from the sea of suph]. KJV Exodus 2:3: “and she laid it in the flags by the river”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:3: וַתָּ֥שֶׂם בַּסּ֖וּף עַל־שְׂפַ֥ת הַיְאֹֽר [and she put it in the suph on the bank of the river]. KJV Jonah 2:5: “the weeds were wrapped about my head”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:6 (KJV 2:5): ס֖וּף חָב֥וּשׁ לְרֹאשִֽׁי [suph was bound to my head]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 10:19: εἰς τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θαλάσσαν [into the Red sea]. 13:18: εἰς τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θάλασσαν [to the Red sea]. 15:4: κατεπόθησαν ἐν ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ [were swallowed up in the Red sea]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/15/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/32/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO10.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO13.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO15.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew name of the sea is made of two words: “sea” and suph. Suph is a word for water plants: the KJV itself has “flags” for it where the infant Moses is laid by the river, and “weeds” where Jonah speaks of the deep. So the Hebrew name says “sea of reeds” or “sea of weeds”. “Red” is a different meaning, and no Hebrew word for red stands in any of these verses. The KJV’s “Red sea” matches the Greek name, not the Hebrew one.

title: One lot for the Lord, the other “for the scapegoat”: for what, or for whom, is the second lot?
summary: Two lots are cast over two goats. One is “for the Lord”. The KJV says the other is “for the scapegoat”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 16:8: κλῆρον ἕνα τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ κλῆρον ἕνα τῷ ἀποπομπαίῳ [one lot for the Lord and one lot for the one of the sending away]. 16:10: ὥστε ἀποστεῖλαι αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν ἀποπομπήν [so as to send it out for the sending away]. 16:26: τὸν χίμαρον τὸν διεσταλμένον εἰς ἄφεσιν [the goat set apart for release]. title: “The morrow after the sabbath”: which sabbath starts the count of fifty days?

title: Seven sevens make forty-nine years; the jubile is the fiftieth. Where does the fiftieth year stand in the count?
summary: Every seventh year the land is not sown. Seven such sevens are forty-nine years, and then the fiftieth year is hallowed and not sown either. Under either reading that keeps it distinct from the forty-ninth, the two consecutive years are unsown.

title: Who buried Moses?
summary: Deuteronomy says of Moses “he buried him” and that no man knows the grave. The verse does not name the one who buried him. Jude speaks of a dispute between Michael and the devil “about the body of Moses” and does not say what the dispute was or who buried the body.
text: KJV Deuteronomy 34:5: “So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord.” KJV 34:6: “And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.” KJV 34:8: “And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days” KJV Jude 1:9: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses” Hebrew (WLC) Deuteronomy 34:6: וַיִּקְבֹּ֨ר אֹתֹ֤ו בַגַּיְ֙ [and he buried him in the valley]; וְלֹֽא־יָדַ֥ע אִישׁ֙ אֶת־קְבֻ֣רָתֹ֔ו עַ֖ד הַיֹּ֥ום הַזֶּֽה [and no man has known his burial place to this day]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/34/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/DEU34.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/65/1/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/65/1/.

Who carried out the burial bears on how the unknown grave is to be understood: a burial by the people who then mourned thirty days might suggest a known grave, while a burial by God is one proposed explanation for its being unknown. title: Rahab’s house was “upon the town wall” — how were the spies sent into it after “the wall fell down flat”?

The verses compared do not say how the house was still there to be entered.

title: What was “the book of Jasher”, and how much of the sun-and-moon passage is taken from it?
summary: In the middle of the account of the sun standing still the text asks, “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” The same book is named once more, at David’s lament. Neither place says what the book was, and Joshua does not mark which of the words around the question are quoted from it.
text: KJV Joshua 10:12: “and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.” KJV 10:13: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.” KJV 10:14: “And there was no day like that before it or after it” KJV 2 Samuel 1:17: “And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son:” KJV 2 Samuel 1:18: “(Also he bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher.)” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 10:13: הֲלֹא־הִ֥יא כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֣פֶר הַיָּשָׁ֑ר [is it not written upon the book of the upright]. 2 Samuel 1:18: הִנֵּ֥ה כְתוּבָ֖ה עַל־סֵ֥פֶר הַיָּשָֽׁר [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 10:13: Καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἐν στάσει, ἕως ἠμύνατο ὁ Θεὸς τοὺς ἐχθροὺς αὐτῶν· καὶ ἔστη ὁ ἥλιος κατὰ μέσον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ [and the sun stood and the moon in their station until God avenged himself on their enemies; and the sun stood in the middle of heaven]. 2 Samuel 1:18: ἰδοὺ γέγραπται ἐπὶ βιβλίου τοῦ εὐθοῦς [behold, it is written upon the book of the upright]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/6/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOS10.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA01.htm.

If the words before it, or the words on both sides of it, are taken from a book of songs, the standing of the sun is being reported in that book’s words; if only the narrator is speaking, the words are attributed to that narrator. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the book was or how much is quoted from it. title: “Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God” — which words, and in which book?
summary: After the covenant at Shechem, Joshua is said to have written “these words in the book of the law of God”. The verse does not say which words he wrote, or whether the book is the book of the law that Moses wrote and had placed beside the ark, which the book of Joshua elsewhere calls “the book of the law of Moses”.
text: KJV Joshua 24:25: “So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem.” KJV 24:26: “And Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God, and took a great stone, and set it up there under an oak, that was by the sanctuary of the Lord.” KJV 24:27: “for it hath heard all the words of the Lord which he spake unto us” KJV 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth” KJV 8:31: “as it is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV 23:6: “all that is written in the book of the law of Moses” KJV Deuteronomy 31:24: “And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,” KJV Deuteronomy 31:26: “Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God” Hebrew (WLC) Joshua 24:26: וַיִּכְתֹּ֤ב יְהֹושֻׁ֙עַ֙ אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה בְּסֵ֖פֶר תֹּורַ֣ת אֱלֹהִ֑ים [and Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God]. 8:31: כַּכָּתוּב֙ בְּסֵ֙פֶר֙ תֹּורַ֣ת מֹשֶׁ֔ה [as it is written in the book of the law of Moses]. Deuteronomy 31:24: לִכְתֹּ֛ב אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֥י הַתֹּורָֽה־הַזֹּ֖את עַל־סֵ֑פֶר עַ֖ד תֻּמָּֽם [to write the words of this law upon a book until they were finished]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Joshua 24:26: Καὶ ἔγραψε τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα εἰς βιβλίον νόμων τοῦ Θεοῦ [and he wrote these words in a book of laws of God]. If it is the same book, Joshua’s writing was added to that book after Moses, without establishing an addition to the substantive law; if it is another book, the passage speaks of a second writing that it does not describe. What “these words” covers — the covenant of that day, its statute and ordinance, or a longer account — is not said either, and it bears on what the passage claims about who wrote what.

title: Judges opens “after the death of Joshua”, then tells of Joshua sending the people away and dying — in what order did these things happen?

title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?
summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. text: KJV Judges 8:23: “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you” KJV 8:24: “I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey” KJV 8:26: “And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold” KJV 8:27: “And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.” KJV 8:33: “as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim” KJV 17:5: “And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim” KJV Exodus 28:4: “And these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe” KJV Exodus 28:6: “And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue, and of purple, of scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cunning work.” KJV 1 Samuel 2:18: “girded with a linen ephod” KJV 1 Samuel 23:9: “he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod” KJV Hosea 3:4: “without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 8:27: וַיַּעַשׂ֩ אֹותֹ֨ו גִדְעֹ֜ון לְאֵפֹ֗וד וַיַּצֵּ֨ג אֹותֹ֤ו בְעִירֹו֙ בְּעָפְרָ֔ה וַיִּזְנ֧וּ כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אַחֲרָ֖יו שָׁ֑ם [and Gideon made it into an ephod and set it in his city, in Ophrah, and all Israel went whoring after it there]. Exodus 28:6: וְעָשׂ֖וּ אֶת־הָאֵפֹ֑ד [and they shall make the ephod]. Exodus 28:6: Καὶ ποιήσουσι τὴν ἐπωμίδα [and they shall make the shoulder-piece]. Gideon’s is made from the collected gold earrings, whose total weight is given as seventeen hundred shekels; the amount used in the ephod is not specified. title: What was the “evil spirit” God sent between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and how did it work?
summary: After three years of Abimelech’s rule “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem”, and the men of Shechem turn on him. The next verse gives the purpose: the blood of Gideon’s sons is to come upon both. The passage does not say what the evil spirit was or how it brought the treachery about.
text: KJV Judges 9:22: “When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel,” KJV 9:23: “Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech:” KJV 9:24: “That the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother” KJV 9:25: “And the men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains” KJV 9:56: “Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech” KJV 9:57: “And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads” KJV 1 Samuel 16:14: “But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:21: “And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:22: “I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” KJV Numbers 5:14: “the spirit of jealousy come upon him” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 9:23: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֱלֹהִים֙ ר֣וּחַ רָעָ֔ה בֵּ֣ין אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ וּבֵ֖ין בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶ֑ם [and God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: רֽוּחַ־רָעָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת יְהוָֽה [an evil spirit from the LORD]. 1 Kings 22:22: ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר [a spirit of falsehood]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 9:23: Καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα πονηρὸν ἀναμέσον Ἀβιμέλεχ καὶ ἀναμέσον τῶν ἀνδρῶν Σικίμων [and God sent out an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: πνεῦμα πονηρὸν παρὰ Κυρίου [an evil spirit from the Lord]. What follows in the story is told as ordinary human action: ambushes in the mountains, a newcomer the men trust, a battle. title: Jephthah “did with her according to his vow” — what was done to his daughter?
summary: Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him “shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering”. His only child comes out. After two months she returns and he “did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man”. Verse 39 reports fulfillment by reference to the vow, without separately describing the act.
text: KJV Judges 11:30: “And Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord” KJV 11:31: “Then it shall be, that whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.” KJV 11:34: “his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances: and she was his only child” KJV 11:35: “for I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back” KJV 11:37: “let me alone two months, that I may go up and down upon the mountains, and bewail my virginity” KJV 11:38: “and bewailed her virginity upon the mountains” KJV 11:39: “And it came to pass at the end of two months, that she returned unto her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man. And it was a custom in Israel,” KJV 11:40: “That the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.” KJV Deuteronomy 12:31: “for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods” KJV 1 Samuel 12:11: “And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you” KJV Hebrews 11:32: “for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 11:31: וְהָיָה֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וְהַעֲלִיתִ֖הוּ עֹולָֽה [and it shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering]. 11:39: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ לָ֔הּ אֶת־נִדְרֹ֖ו אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָדָ֑ר וְהִיא֙ לֹא־יָדְעָ֣ה אִ֔ישׁ [and he did to her his vow which he had vowed; and she had not known a man]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 11:31: καὶ ἔσται τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀνοίσω αὐτὸν ὁλοκαύτωμα [and he shall be the Lord's; I will offer him up as a whole burnt offering]. 11:39: καὶ ἐποίησεν ἐν αὐτῇ τὴν εὐχὴν αὐτοῦ ἣν ηὔξατο· καὶ αὕτη οὐκ ἔγνω ἄνδρα [and he performed on her his vow which he had vowed; and she knew no man]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG11.htm.
reasoning: The vow names a burnt offering, and the fulfilment is told in seven English words that point back to the vow without repeating it. What the passage dwells on instead is her virginity: she asks two months to bewail it, and the report of the fulfilment is followed at once by “and she knew no man”. The reference back to a vow naming a burnt offering provides textual support for the reading that Jephthah sacrificed his daughter. Other readings depend on interpreting the vow or its fulfillment differently. The material question concerns how that reported fulfillment is understood, since verse 39 does not separately describe the act. The verses compared pass no judgement on the act either way.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that Jephthah offered his daughter as a burnt offering, as the words of the vow say; that he gave her to the Lord to live unmarried, a reading that points to the mourning of her virginity and not of her death and to “and she knew no man” after the fulfilment; that the vow had two parts, one for a person and one for a beast, a reading that depends on how the joining word in 11:31 is taken.
